title: Affine neighbourhood transfer for a finite set under an integral finite-fibre cover
statement: Let $Z$ be a locally Noetherian scheme [def-pc-scheme, pqf-def-locnoeth], let $Y$ be a scheme, and let $q:Y\to Z$ be an integral surjective morphism with finite underlying fibres [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. For every finite subset $E\subseteq|Z|$, the following are equivalent: there is an affine open subscheme of $Z$ containing $E$; there is an affine open subscheme of $Y$ containing the entire inverse image $q^{-1}(E)$. Affine means isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. The morphism $q$ need not be flat or finite, and $Y$ need not be locally Noetherian. Empty $E$ is allowed.

source.place: Proposition 4.1.3 (OCR 4.1.5), printed p.55; equivalence for a finite set under an integral surjective morphism with set-theoretically finite fibres. The paper cites Raynaud, Un critere d effectivite de descente, Corollary 5.8. Local archive WANTED; primary scan read at https://www.numdam.org/article/MSMF_1973__33__5_0.pdf

proof.text: If $E=\varnothing$, both conditions hold: the empty open is $\operatorname{Spec}(0)$, since the zero ring has no proper prime ideals. For any $E$, if an affine open $U\subseteq Z$ contains $E$, integrality makes $q$ affine, so $q^{-1}(U)$ is an affine open of $Y$ containing $q^{-1}(E)$. This proves the forward implication, including the empty case.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; necessity and the empty-set edge case (written out)

proof.text: For the converse suppose $E$ is nonempty and $V=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq Y$ is an affine open containing $E\prime=q^{-1}(E)$. Surjectivity makes $E\prime$ nonempty; finite fibres make it finite. Enumerate its primes in $A$ by $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_r$. Set $S=A\setminus\bigcup_i\mathfrak p_i$, a multiplicative subset, and $F\prime=\operatorname{Spec}S^{-1}A$. The scheme $Z$ is quasi-separated because it is locally Noetherian. The integral map $q$ is affine and therefore quasi-separated; thus $Y$ is quasi-separated as well.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; finite inverse image and construction of the semilocalization; avoids the optional separatedness reduction

proof.text: The image of $F\prime\to V$ is the primes disjoint from $S$. A prime $\mathfrak r$ is disjoint from $S$ exactly when $\mathfrak r\subseteq\bigcup_i\mathfrak p_i$, and finite prime avoidance says this is equivalent to $\mathfrak r\subseteq\mathfrak p_i$ for some $i$. Hence its image is $H\prime$, the union of the generalizations of the points of $E\prime$. All those generalizations lie in the open $V$. Here a generalization $a$ of $b$ means $b\in\overline{\{a\}}$.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; the image of the finite-point localization; Stacks Tags 00E3 and 00DS

proof.text: The map $F\prime\to V$ is flat and a monomorphism by the localization leaf. Composing with the open inclusion $V\hookrightarrow Y$ gives a flat monomorphism $j\prime:F\prime\to Y$: its stalk maps are unchanged, and equality of two composites into $Y$ is equality into $V$, hence equality into $F\prime$. Since $F\prime$ is affine it is quasi-compact; since $Y$ is quasi-separated, $j\prime$ is quasi-compact. Thus $H\prime$ is represented by a quasi-compact flat monomorphism, with affine source.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; admissibility upstairs, with the flatness, monomorphism and quasi-compactness checks

proof.text: Let $H$ be the union of the generalizations of points of $E$. Then $q^{-1}(H)=H\prime$. One inclusion follows from continuity. Conversely, take $y$ with $q(y)$ generalizing $e\in E$. The integral morphism $q$ is closed, so the closed subset $q(\overline{\{y\}})$ contains the closure of $\{q(y)\}$ and therefore contains $e$. Consequently some $e\prime\in\overline{\{y\}}$ maps to $e$; it belongs to $E\prime$, and $y$ generalizes $e\prime$. This is a closed-map argument and does not assume flatness or a going-down theorem.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; equality of the two subsets under inverse image

proof.text: Apply integral descent of a subset represented by a quasi-compact flat monomorphism to $q$, $H$, and $j\prime$ of step 4. Its hypotheses hold: $Z$ is locally Noetherian, $q$ is integral and surjective, and step 5 identifies the image of $j\prime$ with $q^{-1}(H)$. It gives a quasi-compact flat monomorphism $j:F\to Z$ with image $H$ and a cartesian square $F\prime\simeq Y\times_ZF$.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; application of Theorem 3.3, including its cartesian identification

proof.text: The projection $p:F\prime\to F$ in that square is surjective, since it is a base change of $q$. It is universally closed: for every further base change to $T\to F$, its pullback is the base change $Y\times_ZT\to T$ of $q$, which is closed because $q$ is integral and hence universally closed. The source $F\prime$ is affine, so the existing surjective-universally-closed affine-target theorem (Stacks Tag 05YU) proves that $F$ is affine.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; affineness downstairs; the existing 05YU node subsumes the source's Chevalley application

proof.text: Apply the quasi-affine neighbourhood theorem to $j:F\to Z$. The map is a quasi-compact flat monomorphism by step 6; $F$ is affine by step 7, hence is itself a quasi-compact open subscheme of an affine scheme; and $Z$ is quasi-separated by step 2. We obtain a quasi-compact quasi-affine open $U\subseteq Z$ containing $H$, and hence containing $E$. Choose an isomorphism of $U$ with an open subscheme $W$ of an affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}B$, as supplied by the meaning of quasi-affine.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; application of Proposition 3.4

proof.text: Write $\operatorname{Spec}B\setminus W=V(J)$ for an ideal $J$; this is the definition of a Zariski closed subset of a spectrum. The finitely many points of $E$ correspond to primes $\mathfrak m_i\in W$. Thus $J\not\subseteq\mathfrak m_i$ for every $i$. Finite prime avoidance gives $b\in J$ outside all the $\mathfrak m_i$. The principal open $D(b)$ contains these points, is contained in $W$, and is affine. Transporting it through $W\simeq U$ gives an affine open of $Z$ containing $E$, as required.

source.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15; last sentence: finite points in a quasi-affine scheme; explicit prime-avoidance argument (Stacks Tag 00DS)

proof_origin.place: Corollary 3.8, printed p.15, with Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 3.4. Primary scan read online; archive WANTED. Agent supplies explicit semilocalization, closed-map argument and final prime avoidance, and uses the existing Stacks 05YU node for affine descent.
